summary: Defines SNMP management objects for devices that implement FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network technology. It gives network managers a standard set of variables for monitoring FDDI stations. The RFC has historic status.

eli5.summary: A report card for a fast ring of glass cables. It lists the things a network helper can ask FDDI equipment about, so different makers all answer the same way.

questions: how to manage fddi with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management objects for FDDI fiber-ring stations, drawn from the ANSI SMT standard.

tldr.problem: Managers using SNMP needed a standard way to monitor devices that implement FDDI, and manufacturers wanted to share instrumentation with other management schemes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the FDDI MIB under { transmission 15 }, recasting the mandatory ANSI X3T9.5 SMT variables as SNMP objects in groups for SMT, MAC, PATH, PORT, ATTACHMENT and chip sets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1285 now has Historic status and was updated by RFC 1512.

facts.label: Groups
facts.value: SMT, MAC, PATH, PORT, ATTACHMENT, Chip Sets

today: RFC 1285 has Historic status and was updated by RFC 1512. Use the later document, not this one, as the FDDI MIB definition.

sections.title: Purpose and Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing devices that implement FDDI. It sits within the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: the SMI (RFC 1155, with RFC 1212 as a more concise form), the MIB (RFC 1156 and RFC 1213) and SNMP (RFC 1157).

As with other MIB modules, each object has a name (an object identifier), a syntax written in a restricted subset of ASN.1, and an encoding that uses the ASN.1 basic encoding rules.
sections.eli5: It is a menu of questions you can ask FDDI network equipment, written in the standard menu style everyone already uses.

sections.title: Relationship to the ANSI SMT Standard
sections.content:
The module applies to interfaces whose ifType is fddi(15), and the FDDI subtree is { transmission 15 }. Its definitions draw heavily from the ANSI X3T9.5 committee and its SMT subcommittee, and are identical to the ANSI ones to the maximum extent possible.

Only syntax was changed, for example remapping booleans to enumerated integers and bit strings to octet strings, and some names. The goal was to let SNMP-manageable FDDI systems share instrumentation with other management schemes, and to ease translating information between them. Only the variables that are mandatory in the ANSI specification were kept, because optional ones were seen as less widely accepted.
sections.eli5: The questions were copied from the FDDI builders' own rulebook, with only the wording changed so the network helper's tools can read them.

sections.title: Textual Conventions and Groups
sections.content:
Several textual conventions are introduced to make the module easier to read and compare with the ANSI text. They change neither syntax nor semantics. Examples:

  • FddiTime: an integer in octet units of 80 nanoseconds, used for path latency and synchronous bandwidth.
  • FddiResourceId: refers to a MAC, PORT, PATH or ATTACHMENT resource. Indexing begins at 1 and zero means the absence of a resource.
  • FddiSMTStationIdType: an 8-octet station identifier whose low-order six octets come from a unique IEEE-assigned address.
  • FddiMACLongAddressType: a 6-octet MAC address in IEEE canonical notation.

The objects fall into six groups under the fddi node: SMT, MAC, PATH, PORT, ATTACHMENT and Chip Sets. The SMT, MAC, PORT and ATTACHMENT groups are mandatory for all systems that implement manageable FDDI subsystems. The PATH group is empty for now, until the ANSI community settles its own PATH group. The Chip Set group only allocates object identifiers for PHY and MAC chip sets, and none are defined at present.
sections.eli5: The questions are sorted into folders: one for the whole station, one for each network card, one for each plug, and so on. A few special kinds of answers, like a time or a station name, get their own rules.

sections.title: SMT, MAC, PORT and ATTACHMENT Objects
sections.content:
Each group has a table with one row per instance, and most objects carry an ANSI reference. The SMT group starts with snmpFddiSMTNumber, the number of SMT implementations, and a table with the station ID, the operating, highest and lowest SMT version, the counts of MACs, master ports and non-master ports, configuration capabilities and policy, and state values such as the ECM and CF states, plus a station action.

The MAC, PORT and ATTACHMENT groups follow the same pattern, holding per-interface objects defined for the corresponding ANSI resources. Some objects are read-only, while others, such as the operating SMT version, are read-write.
sections.eli5: For each part of the equipment, the network helper can ask who it is, what it can do, and what it is doing right now. A few settings can also be changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo, and it adds no security guidance of its own for the objects it defines.
sections.eli5: The note says nothing about keeping this information safe.
